summary:
LIFTOFF is an educational space-mission design game for ages 7–13, created for NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026. Players choose an Earth, Moon, or Mars mission, build a modular spacecraft, select instruments and ground stations, complete launch checks, simulate the mission, and receive a clear report explaining the outcome.

The game makes real mission-planning trade-offs understandable: every choice affects mass, power, fuel, cost, data, communications, and time. Its calculations and catalog values are based on NASA/JPL sources, while visual gauges, warnings, and step-by-step guidance turn complex engineering into hands-on learning.

LIFTOFF matters because it helps young people see that space exploration is not magic—it is creative problem-solving, teamwork, and evidence-based decision-making.
details:
LIFTOFF is a Java-based educational game that lets children design and fly science missions to Earth orbit, the Moon, and Mars. Players move through a guided workflow: read a mission briefing, assemble a spacecraft from modular parts, choose instruments and ground stations, check resources, launch, simulate the flight, and review a report explaining what worked and what should change. Every decision has consequences. Heavier payloads affect mass and fuel, instruments consume power and create data, ground stations determine how much data returns home, and budgets and timelines limit the design. The game uses sourced NASA/JPL-inspired mission data and models concepts such as orbit coverage, launch capacity, fuel requirements, and mission trade-offs. Its intended impact is to make systems engineering and space science approachable for ages 7–13, encouraging curiosity, experimentation, and learning from failure without oversimplifying real constraints. Technology used: Java 21 JavaFX 21 FXML CSS Maven Jackson JSON catalogs JUnit 5 JavaFX 3D rendering NASA-based imagery/model The project is creative because it turns genuine aerospace design constraints into a colourful, interactive mission game with modular ships, drag-and-drop choices, simulations, feedback gauges, and redesign loops. Our team considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, child-friendly interaction, visual clarity, source attribution, testability, and separation between game rules and the user interface.
